cards.a: Roaming is a client moving from one AP/BSS to another while keeping its session. Types differ by scope: Layer 2 vs Layer 3, intra- versus inter-WLC, plus 802.11r fast roaming for handoff speed. Roaming works because mobility (a mobility group) shares the client state.

cards.q: What are the roaming types and their scopes?
cards.a: Layer 2 roaming stays on the same subnet (switch path); Layer 3 roaming crosses to a different subnet and needs anchor forwarding; intra-WLC roaming is within one controller; inter-WLC roaming crosses controllers via mobility.

cards.q: What happens during a roaming handoff?
cards.a: The client reassociates with the new AP at its new BSSID, the WLC/mobility state updates, frames follow the client, and the old AP releases it.
802.11r (fast transition, FT) pre-distributes a PMK so reassociation is fast, giving millisecond-level handoffs ideal for voice/real-time traffic.
802.11k provides neighbor reports and 802.11v assists client roaming, together helping clients pick the right AP in a network-driven way.

cards.q: What are sticky clients and how do you fix them?
cards.a: A sticky client hangs on a weak AP because of the RSSI threshold or missing steering. Fixes are 802.11v/disabling, band steering for RF utilization, and 802.11r for slow handoffs. Band steering plus 802.11k/v/r fixes stickiness and slow handoffs.

cards.q: What is required for seamless roaming?
cards.a: The same SSID (an ESS), the same security (PMK/802.1X), shared state (mobility group), and fast keys (802.11r). All must line up for a zero-drama roam.

cards.q: What commands verify clients and roaming?
cards.a: show wireless client summary, show wireless client mac <MAC>, show ap summary, show wireless mobility client, and debug dot11 for dot11 details.

cards.q: Roam sessions drop or roam slowly. What are the likely causes and checks?
cards.a: Session drops usually mean the reassociation failed (check show wireless client summary); slow roam usually means 802.11r is not enabled, so check the FT config.

cards.q: Clients stick to weak APs, cross-L3 roams fail, and there is a reauth loop. What should you check?
cards.a: Sticky clients come from RSSI issues, fixed with band steering; cross-L3 failures point to the anchor/mobility path; a reauth loop indicates a key mismatch in security.

cards.q: How do Layer 2 and Layer 3 roaming differ?
cards.a: A Layer 2 roam stays on the same subnet; a Layer 3 roam moves to a different subnet and requires the anchor WLC to forward traffic.

cards.q: What is the difference between 802.11r and 802.11k/v?
cards.a: 802.11r provides fast keys (fast transition/FT) for quick handoffs, while 802.11k provides neighbor reports and 802.11v assists roaming — together they help clients choose the right AP.

cards.q: Which Roaming quick review facts should you remember?
cards.a: L2 roam is same subnet, L3 needs the anchor path; intra-WLC is one controller, inter-WLC uses mobility; 802.11r gives fast keys, 802.11k/v assist and neighbor reports; sticky clients are fixed with band steering; seamless roaming needs the same SSID.
